info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 13.1: Formulating Editorial Principles, Methodology, and the Edition Introduction.

name.text: 01 Question: Entering the Studio: The Capstone Digital Scholarly Edition

questiontext.text: What is the primary goal of Week 13's capstone publication studio?

generalfeedback.text: Week 13 brings together all your semester projects into an integrated, publication-grade digital scholarly edition.

answer.text: To bring together all eight semester editorial layers into a unified, publication-grade digital scholarly edition.

feedback.text: Correct. Week 13 integrates transcription, normalization, lemmatization, named entities, alignment, and commentary into a coherent edition.

answer.text: To begin a brand new course on video game animation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Week 13 is the capstone studio for our historical document editing course.

answer.text: To delete all previous assignments to prepare for the winter semester.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Students synthesize their semester research rather than deleting it.

answer.text: To replace primary archival witnesses with modern textbooks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The edition showcases primary historical witnesses.

name.text: 02 Question: The Anatomy of a Digital Edition Portfolio

questiontext.text: Which TEI XML element serves as the container for scholarly commentary notes in our digital edition architecture?

generalfeedback.text: A digital edition combines eight distinct editorial layers into a single structured master document.

answer.text: The container, which keeps editorial interpretation cleanly separated from the primary text.

feedback.text: Correct. The element houses interpretive commentary notes without interrupting the primary diplomatic text body.

answer.text: The element alone.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The teiHeader contains metadata and cataloguing, while standoff holds commentary.

answer.text: The container.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The facsimile element binds digital page images.

answer.text: The element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The titleStmt declares titles and authors within the header.

name.text: 03 Question: The Purpose of the Editorial Introduction

questiontext.text: Why must an editor author an Editorial Introduction for their digital scholarly edition?

generalfeedback.text: The editorial introduction sets up context, explains document history, and makes editorial decisions transparent to readers.

answer.text: To establish authority, explain historical context, document the physical witness, and make editorial rules transparent.

feedback.text: Correct. Without an introduction, readers cannot determine why a document matters or how the text was edited.

answer.text: To increase the word count of the repository to win a contest.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Introductions provide essential scholarly context, not artificial word counts.

answer.text: Because Canadian copyright law mandates a 10,000-word introduction for all student papers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Introductions fulfill academic scholarship standards, not copyright length mandates.

answer.text: To conceal the names of the historical authors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Introductions document and celebrate historical authors and their witnesses.

name.text: 04 Question: The Twofold Introduction: Narrative Preface vs Machine Metadata

questiontext.text: How do the two forms of the digital introduction differ in audience and format?

generalfeedback.text: Digital editions provide a twofold introduction: narrative prose for human readers and structured XML metadata for machines.

answer.text: The narrative preface is a readable essay for human scholars, while the TEI header contains machine-actionable XML metadata for software.

feedback.text: Correct. Humans read the narrative preface, while search engines and digital humanities tools process the structured TEI header.

answer.text: The narrative preface is written in Latin, while the XML header is written in French.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Language choice is governed by scholarship, not an arbitrary language split.

answer.text: The narrative preface is deleted after grading, while the XML header is published.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both components are published as permanent parts of the digital edition.

answer.text: The narrative preface contains only numbers, while the header contains only pictures.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both forms present rich contextual and methodological information.

name.text: 05 Question: The Single-Witness Documentary Edition

questiontext.text: Why does our 2026 cohort create single-witness documentary editions rather than multi-witness stemmata?

generalfeedback.text: Our cohort creates single-witness documentary editions, prioritizing deep fidelity to individual historical artifacts over multi-witness collation.

answer.text: Because each student edits a unique historical artifact requiring deep codicological fidelity rather than reconstructing a lost ancestor.

feedback.text: Correct. Documentary editions represent individual archival witnesses with complete fidelity to physical ink and layout.

answer.text: Because multi-witness collation was permanently outlawed by the TEI Consortium.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Collation is standard TEI practice for multi-witness traditions, but our cohort works with single witnesses.

answer.text: Because computers crash when attempting to process more than one text file at a time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modern computers process thousands of texts simultaneously.

answer.text: Because historical manuscripts never survive in more than one copy.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Many ancient works survive in dozens of copies, but our cohort's projects are unique documents.

name.text: 06 Question: Introducing Ace's Witness: 1791 French Revolutionary Decree

questiontext.text: What primary historical problem did the May 1791 assignat decree address during the French Revolution?

generalfeedback.text: Ace's introduction frames the 1791 decree within the French Revolution's monetary collapse, paper assignats, and royal legal sanction.

answer.text: A severe shortage of small-denomination currency for daily wages and food purchases, addressed by authorizing 5-livre notes.

feedback.text: Correct. Early assignats were only printed in massive sums, making daily commerce impossible for common workers.

answer.text: A shortage of printing ink at the Imprimerie Royale.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The decree addressed monetary liquidity and small currency, not ink supplies.

answer.text: King Louis XVI's refusal to sign any document written in French.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The King signed French legislation until his overthrow in 1792.

answer.text: An invasion of Paris by British naval warships.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Paris is an inland city and was not invaded by warships in May 1791.

name.text: 07 Question: Introducing Olyvia's Witness: 1967 Maud Lewis Letter

questiontext.text: What cultural reality of Maud Lewis's life should Olyvia's introduction emphasize?

generalfeedback.text: Olyvia's introduction highlights Maud Lewis's daily life, modest pricing, folk spelling, and personal correspondence with collector Leonard Kinnear.

answer.text: Her modest pricing of \$6.00 per painting sold from her home, despite growing national fame following CBC television broadcasts.

feedback.text: Correct. Maud Lewis maintained humble roadside and mail pricing despite widespread national attention.

answer.text: Her international career managing corporate commercial galleries in Paris.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Maud Lewis lived simply in Marshalltown and never managed European galleries.

answer.text: Her secret identity as a Canadian federal cabinet minister.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Maud Lewis was an internationally celebrated Nova Scotia folk painter.

answer.text: Her complete refusal to correspond with anyone outside Digby County.

feedback.text: Incorrect. She corresponded with collectors across Canada, including Leonard Kinnear in Moncton.

name.text: 08 Question: Introducing Andromeda's Witness: 1752 Peace and Friendship Treaty

questiontext.text: What key provision did the 1752 Treaty at Halifax establish regarding Mi'kmaw resource rights?

generalfeedback.text: Andromeda's introduction documents the 1752 treaty negotiations between Chief Cope and Governor Hopson, emphasizing ongoing Mi'kmaw resource rights.

answer.text: It recognized the 'free liberty of Hunting and Fishing as usual' and established a regulated government trading post (truckhouse).

feedback.text: Correct. The 1752 Treaty confirmed ongoing resource harvesting and regulated commercial trade between Mi'kmaq and British authorities.

answer.text: It required the Mi'kmaq to relocate permanently to Great Britain.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The treaty governed peace and trade within traditional Mi'kmaw territory in Nova Scotia.

answer.text: It banned all trading between Indigenous people and colonial merchants.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The treaty explicitly promoted regulated trade through truckhouses.

answer.text: It declared that Nova Scotia would become a colony of Spain.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Nova Scotia was a British crown colony in 1752.

name.text: 09 Question: Describing the Physical Artifact in sourceDesc and msDesc

questiontext.text: Where in the TEI header are the repository name, call number, and physical dimensions recorded?

generalfeedback.text: Use msDesc inside sourceDesc to record the repository, shelfmark, physical support, and dimensions of your document.

answer.text: Inside the element, structured within , , and .

feedback.text: Correct. The module provides structured containers for repository identifiers and physical codicology.

answer.text: Inside the change logs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. RevisionDesc tracks file editing history, not physical artifact metadata.

answer.text: Scattered inside footnote elements in the text body.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Physical manuscript descriptions belong in the TEI header.

answer.text: In a separate Microsoft Excel spreadsheet outside the project.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI embeds codicological descriptions directly within the master XML header.

name.text: 10 Question: Documenting Materiality: Parchment, Paper, Seals, and Ink

questiontext.text: Why is documenting material details like paper chain lines, wax seals, and ink types valuable in a digital edition?

generalfeedback.text: Describing paper, ink, and wax seals connects digital readers to the physical craftsmanship of historical documents.

answer.text: It connects digital readers to the physical craftsmanship, legal authenticity, and material context of the original artifact.

feedback.text: Correct. Describing material features preserves codicological evidence that flat screen pixels might otherwise obscure.

answer.text: Because digital files cannot be opened unless the user knows the chemical formula of the ink.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML parsers process text without chemical formulas.

answer.text: To allow students to manufacture counterfeit historical documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly editing promotes historical research, not forgery.

answer.text: Because wax seals contain computer microchips that store data.

feedback.text: Incorrect. 18th-century wax seals are physical wax impressions, not electronic chips.

name.text: 11 Question: Documenting Provenance and Archival Custody

questiontext.text: What is the scholarly purpose of the element inside the TEI header?

generalfeedback.text: Provenance documents how a manuscript traveled from its historical creator to modern archives and collections.

answer.text: To document the historical chain of custody from the original creator through private owners to modern archival repositories.

feedback.text: Correct. Provenance establishes document authenticity by tracing its ownership and preservation history over time.

answer.text: To calculate how many miles the manuscript traveled on an airplane.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Provenance records historical ownership and archival custody, not flight mileage.

answer.text: To record the bank account numbers of private manuscript collectors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Financial account details must never be stored in scholarly metadata.

answer.text: To determine which student types the fastest in the computer lab.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Provenance pertains to historical artifact custody.

name.text: 12 Question: The TEI Editorial Declaration: editorialDecl

questiontext.text: What is the function of the element in the TEI header?

generalfeedback.text: The editorialDecl element declares your explicit rules for transcription, correction, and normalization, ensuring scholarly trust.

answer.text: It declares explicit policies governing transcription fidelity, spelling normalization, correction, and annotation scope.

feedback.text: Correct. The editorial declaration serves as the methodological contract explaining all editorial choices to the reader.

answer.text: It automatically submits student grades to the university registrar.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The editorial declaration is scholarly metadata, not an administrative grading tool.

answer.text: It deletes any spelling mistake without notifying the reader.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editorial declarations make changes explicit and transparent.

answer.text: It changes the background color of the operating system.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editorial declarations contain text-critical metadata.

name.text: 13 Question: The correction Element: Handling Errors and Emendations

questiontext.text: In the TEI declaration, what does the attribute method='markup' signify?

generalfeedback.text: The correction element explains how scribal slips and typographical errors were identified, preserved, or corrected.

answer.text: That corrections are applied using explicit TEI tags (like ) rather than silently altering the source text.

feedback.text: Correct. Method='markup' indicates that both original and corrected readings remain visible in the XML tree.

answer.text: That the editor used a red felt-tip marker on the original parchment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholars never deface physical archival manuscripts.

answer.text: That the document was converted into an uncompressed audio file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Method='markup' describes digital XML tagging conventions.

answer.text: That the editor refused to correct any errors under any circumstances.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Method='markup' indicates that corrections were made via transparent tags.

name.text: 14 Question: The normalization Element: Articulating Regularization Rules

questiontext.text: Why must the element provide concrete examples of regularized historical spellings?

generalfeedback.text: The normalization element documents regularized spelling patterns, such as updating eighteenth-century verb endings.

answer.text: To provide readers and search software with exact rules on how archaic variants (like -oit to -ait) were modernized.

feedback.text: Correct. Clear rules ensure that searches across regularized text behave predictably and transparently.

answer.text: Because readers will be fined if they misspell historical French verbs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Academic documentation serves clarity, not financial penalties.

answer.text: To prove that eighteenth-century scribes were uneducated.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical spelling reflected contemporary conventions, not lack of education.

answer.text: Because TEI schemas reject any document with fewer than fifty examples.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schemas validate XML structure, not arbitrary quota counts.

name.text: 15 Question: The quotation and hyphenation Elements

questiontext.text: How does declaring hyphenation rules (e.g. eol='all' and ) help digital edition users?

generalfeedback.text: Declare quotation and hyphenation rules so readers understand how line breaks and spoken dialogue are handled.

answer.text: It clarifies whether words split across line breaks are preserved with hyphens or rejoined for digital full-text searching.

feedback.text: Correct. Proper hyphenation markup preserves lineation while allowing search engines to match compound words.

answer.text: It permanently deletes all hyphens from the English language.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hyphenation rules govern specific document formatting.

answer.text: It forces web browsers to display all text in a single vertical column.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Layout rendering is controlled by CSS, not hyphenation metadata.

answer.text: It prevents readers from copying and pasting text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI editions promote accessible, reusable scholarship.

name.text: 16 Question: The interpretation Element: Defining Annotation Scope

questiontext.text: What should an editor define inside the element of their editorial declaration?

generalfeedback.text: The interpretation element explains the categories, purpose, and standoff architecture of your commentary notes.

answer.text: The thematic categories, scholarly purpose, and standoff architecture of their commentary notes.

feedback.text: Correct. The interpretation element explains the taxonomy and research goals guiding explanatory notes.

answer.text: Their personal political opinions about modern elections.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editorial declarations pertain to the historical edition, not modern partisan politics.

answer.text: The names of all movie actors who starred in historical films.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commentary declarations focus on the primary textual witness.

answer.text: The daily weather forecast for Halifax during the exam period.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editorial paratexts document scholarship, not meteorology.

name.text: 17 Question: Stating Linguistic Policies: Lemmas, Glosses, and Dictionaries

questiontext.text: Why is citing specific historical dictionaries (like the 1798 Academy dictionary or the OED) essential in your introduction?

generalfeedback.text: Citing authoritative historical dictionaries in your introduction validates your linguistic lemmas and grammatical glosses.

answer.text: It establishes the empirical authority behind your lemmatizations and grammatical glosses, proving they reflect historical usage.

feedback.text: Correct. Grounding linguistic analysis in authoritative dictionaries ensures that definitions reflect historical reality.

answer.text: Because digital editions are required to purchase advertisements for dictionary publishers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Citing scholarly dictionaries is academic attribution, not commercial marketing.

answer.text: To prove that historical words have never changed their meanings over time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Languages evolve continuously; historical dictionaries document that evolution.

answer.text: Because XML parsers crash if they cannot connect to an online dictionary API.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML files are standalone documents that do not depend on external APIs to validate.

name.text: 18 Question: Stating Named Entity and Authority Control Policies

questiontext.text: How should an editorial introduction address historical figures who lack official records in global authority databases like VIAF?

generalfeedback.text: Document your authority control strategy, explaining how historical entities are linked to Wikidata, VIAF, or local archive records.

answer.text: By explaining that unlisted individuals are identified through local archival records, while prominent figures link to Wikidata QIDs.

feedback.text: Correct. A mature digital edition accounts for both prominent figures and historically marginalized local individuals.

answer.text: By deleting unlisted people from the historical transcription.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editors never erase real historical people from primary sources.

answer.text: By inventing fake authority records with fabricated numbers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Fabricating authority identifiers violates academic integrity.

answer.text: By claiming that all people without Wikipedia pages never existed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Most historical people lived without modern encyclopedic entries.

name.text: 19 Question: Stating Commentary Policies: Documenting AI Assistance and HITL Vetting

questiontext.text: What is the required standard for disclosing generative AI assistance in a scholarly digital edition?

generalfeedback.text: The introduction must explicitly disclose AI assistance, describing the verification protocols used to ensure historical accuracy.

answer.text: Explicitly disclosing the AI model used, describing the prompt guardrails, and documenting human verification protocols in the method statement.

feedback.text: Correct. Academic integrity requires transparent disclosure of AI drafting tools alongside proof of human editorial verification.

answer.text: Pretending the AI model was a human co-author with a faculty appointment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI models are software tools, not human academic authors.

answer.text: Concealing AI assistance completely to avoid academic scrutiny.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Secret AI use constitutes academic dishonesty.

answer.text: Refusing to publish any edition that touched a computer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Computational methods are welcomed when practiced transparently and critically.

name.text: 20 Question: The Editorial Method Statement: Ethical Transparency

questiontext.text: What is the purpose of an Editorial Method Statement in a capstone digital edition?

generalfeedback.text: The Editorial Method Statement synthesizes your transcription, normalization, annotation, and verification principles into a clear public manifesto.

answer.text: To synthesize all transcription, normalization, annotation, and verification principles into a clear, unified public manifesto.

feedback.text: Correct. The method statement articulates the editor's overarching philosophy, making their scholarship transparent and reproducible.

answer.text: To serve as a legal waiver preventing readers from criticizing the edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarship invites peer critique and review.

answer.text: To list the retail price of printed copies of the edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Method statements articulate scholarly principles, not retail pricing.

answer.text: To replace the need for providing any primary text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The method statement introduces and accompanies the primary text.

name.text: 21 Question: Licensing and Copyright in publicationStmt

questiontext.text: What legal problem occurs if a digital edition is published without a license in ?

generalfeedback.text: Declare publisher, publication date, and open access licensing in publicationStmt to make your edition legally reusable.

answer.text: The edition exists under 'all rights reserved' by default, creating legal uncertainty that prevents other scholars from reusing the data.

feedback.text: Correct. Declaring an open license grants explicit legal permission for researchers to study and build upon your XML data.

answer.text: The computer hard drive automatically erases itself after forty-eight hours.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lack of a license creates legal ambiguity, not hardware failure.

answer.text: The university police immediately confiscate the student's laptop.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Licensing is an intellectual property standard, not a criminal matter.

answer.text: The document is automatically translated into ancient Greek.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Licensing affects legal reuse rights, not language translation.

name.text: 22 Question: Choosing an Open Access License: Creative Commons (CC BY / CC0)

questiontext.text: In multi-tiered licensing, which license is recommended for catalogue metadata and XML schemas to ensure maximum library discovery?

generalfeedback.text: Use CC BY for editorial prose, CC0 for catalogue metadata, and MIT for scripts to enable open scholarship.

answer.text: Creative Commons Zero (CC0 1.0 Public Domain Dedication), allowing unrestricted global harvesting by library systems.

feedback.text: Correct. CC0 waives copyright restrictions on metadata, allowing global library catalogs to index your edition freely.

answer.text: Strict All Rights Reserved commercial copyright.

feedback.text: Incorrect. All Rights Reserved prevents open library catalog harvesting.

answer.text: A commercial patent held by Apple or Google.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital editions are scholarly works, not commercial hardware patents.

answer.text: A secret nondisclosure agreement signed by the instructor.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Open access scholarship promotes public discovery rather than secrecy.

name.text: 23 Question: Organizing the Capstone Project Repository in VS Code

questiontext.text: Why is a clean folder structure (separating XML sources, web players, and PDF outputs) vital in a project repository?

generalfeedback.text: Organize your project into clear folders for XML sources, web players, PDF deliverables, and license documentation.

answer.text: It ensures that transformation scripts run smoothly and allows external scholars to navigate your edition easily on GitHub.

feedback.text: Correct. Consistent directory organization is essential for automated build pipelines and open research collaboration.

answer.text: Because disorganized folders cause laptops to overheat and catch fire.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Folder organization affects workflow clarity, not hardware temperature.

answer.text: Because GitHub deletes repositories that contain more than three folders.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GitHub supports deeply nested directory structures.

answer.text: To hide your primary XML files from your classmates.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Repositories are designed for transparent sharing and peer review.

name.text: 24 Question: Master File Structure: Combining Header, Text, and Standoff

questiontext.text: What are the three primary child elements directly under the root element in our master edition?

generalfeedback.text: The canonical TEI master document combines teiHeader, facsimile, text body, and standOff commentary in a single XML file.

answer.text: <teiHeader> (metadata and policies), <text> (primary body transcription), and <standOff> (commentary notes).

feedback.text: Correct. This tripartite architecture cleanly separates document metadata, primary transcription, and interpretive research.

answer.text: <title>, <author>, and <date>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are sub-elements inside the header, not primary children of root TEI.

answer.text: <html>, <head>, and <body>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are standard HTML web elements, not TEI P5 elements.

answer.text: <file1>, <file2>, and <file3>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI uses semantic element names established by international guidelines.

name.text: 25 Question: Validating the Master TEI File Against Schema

questiontext.text: What does a green validation checkmark in VS Code indicate when checking your master TEI XML file?

generalfeedback.text: Run schema validation in VS Code to ensure well-formed tags, unique identifiers, and valid pointer references.

answer.text: That your XML markup is well-formed, contains unique identifiers, and strictly adheres to the official TEI Relax NG schema rules.

feedback.text: Correct. Validation confirms that your digital edition complies with international standards without syntax errors.

answer.text: That your historical essay has received a final grade of 100%.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schema validation verifies technical syntax, not qualitative grading.

answer.text: That the computer battery is fully charged.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Validation checkmarks indicate XML compliance, not battery status.

answer.text: That all historical people mentioned in the document are still alive.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Technical validators inspect code structure, not biological longevity.

name.text: 26 Question: Writing a Project README.md for External Scholars

questiontext.text: Why is the project README.md called the 'digital front door' of your edition repository?

generalfeedback.text: The project README.md welcomes visitors, summarizes document history, provides quick viewing links, and provides citation formats.

answer.text: Because it is the first file displayed when visitors arrive at your repository, welcoming readers and explaining how to explore the edition.

feedback.text: Correct. A well-crafted README orients visitors, provides viewing links, and outlines project goals.

answer.text: Because it locks the repository so that nobody can view the files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The README invites visitors rather than locking files.

answer.text: Because it acts as a physical wooden door on the computer screen.

feedback.text: Incorrect. 'Front door' is a metaphor for welcoming introductory documentation.

answer.text: Because it only works when accessed from a front porch.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The README can be accessed globally on any web connection.

name.text: 27 Question: Peer Reviewing the Editorial Introduction

questiontext.text: How does exchanging editorial introductions with a classmate during peer review improve your edition?

generalfeedback.text: Peer review helps editors identify missing archival details and clarify editorial principles before final publication.

answer.text: It allows an outside reader to identify missing archival shelfmarks, vague normalization rules, or unclear historical context before final submission.

feedback.text: Correct. Peer review catches oversights and ensures that your principles are understandable to other scholars.

answer.text: It allows students to copy each other's homework without doing any research.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Peer review provides constructive feedback on unique individual projects.

answer.text: It forces both students to change their primary historical documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Peer review refines documentation without changing project witnesses.

answer.text: It automatically publishes the edition in a major academic journal.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Classroom peer review prepares students for formal scholarly publication standards.

name.text: 28 Question: Common Flaws in Student Editorial Introductions

questiontext.text: Which common beginner mistake undermines the scholarly trust of an editorial introduction?

generalfeedback.text: Avoid common beginner errors by providing specific shelfmarks, concrete normalization examples, and verified XML pointers.

answer.text: Failing to provide the exact archival repository name, shelfmark, and call number for the primary witness.

feedback.text: Correct. An edition without archival shelfmarks cannot be verified against the physical artifact.

answer.text: Using 12-point font instead of 11-point font in notes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Font size is a styling choice, not an epistemological flaw.

answer.text: Writing in complete, grammatical English sentences.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Clear, grammatical writing is the hallmark of good scholarship.

answer.text: Citing authoritative historical dictionaries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Citing authoritative dictionaries strengthens an edition.

name.text: 29 Question: Checklists for Editorial Completeness

questiontext.text: Why should editors work through an editorial completeness checklist before moving to visual presentation styling?

generalfeedback.text: Use an editorial checklist to confirm that all historical, material, and policy declarations are complete and valid.

answer.text: To ensure that all historical context, material descriptions, normalization policies, and licenses are valid before writing CSS styles.

feedback.text: Correct. Sound editorial content must be established before designing presentation stylesheets.

answer.text: To delay finishing the assignment as long as possible.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Checklists keep work organized and prevent missed deadlines.

answer.text: Because university servers reject files that lack a checklist.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Checklists are human quality assurance workflows.

answer.text: To avoid having to write any XML code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Checklists verify that XML code is complete and compliant.

name.text: 30 Question: Synthesis: Preparing for Presentation Styling in Lesson 13.2

questiontext.text: What is the next step in our capstone studio after formulating editorial principles in Lesson 13.1?

generalfeedback.text: Having formulated editorial principles in Lesson 13.1, you are ready to style your edition for the web in Lesson 13.2.

answer.text: Exploring the TEI Processing Model and mapping semantic XML tags to visual web presentation using CSS in Lesson 13.2.

feedback.text: Correct. Lesson 13.2 takes your validated XML master and styles it for interactive web display.

answer.text: Deleting all XML markup and writing the edition in plain notepad.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lesson 13.2 builds directly upon your TEI master markup.

answer.text: Printing the entire internet onto paper.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital humanities focuses on curated, sustainable publishing.

answer.text: Skipping the rest of the semester to take a vacation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The course concludes with the publication of your capstone edition portfolio.
